Exit code 1
# CMJ measurement properties in D1 football: what these metrics can and cannot see

**Status:** analysis complete
**Data:** 185 athletes, 92,550 athlete-metric-days, 5,930 retest pairs per metric, 2023–2025
**Reproduce:** `python -m src.research.measurement`

## Why this comes first

Ward's framing puts measurement ahead of modelling — validity, reliability,
responsiveness — because a metric that cannot resolve a meaningful change will
return a null regardless of how well the study is designed.

We arrived here the hard way. Six separate attempts to detect a practice-load
effect on readiness returned nothing. Before concluding that practice load has
no effect, we checked whether our instruments could have seen one.

## Method

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Typical error (TE)** | SD(difference) / √2 across consecutive **same-weekday** tests ≤10 days apart |
| **SWC** | 0.2 × between-athlete SD (conventional smallest worthwhile change) |
| **SWC / TE** | Below 1, the metric cannot resolve a worthwhile change even in principle |

Same-weekday pairing is deliberate. Monday and Thursday sit at different points
in the training week, so pooling them would charge real weekly rhythm to
measurement noise and overstate TE.

## Results

| Metric | TE % | SWC/TE | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concentric Impulse | 2.9 | 0.99 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Peak Power / BM | 3.8 | 0.78 | cannot resolve SWC |
| P1 Concentric Impulse | 4.8 | 0.69 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Jump Height (Imp-Mom) | 5.7 | 0.63 | cannot resolve SWC |
| P2 Concentric Impulse | 6.3 | 0.57 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Concentric Impulse-100ms | 8.4 | 0.50 | cannot resolve SWC |
| **RSI-modified** | **8.8** | **0.48** | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Duration | 6.6 | 0.42 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Deceleration RFD / BM | 18.4 | 0.42 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Peak Power / BM | 13.4 | 0.34 | cannot resolve SWC |

**None of the ten metrics resolves the smallest worthwhile change at
individual, week-to-week resolution.**

## Two caveats, both of which make this less damning than it reads

1. **TE here is week-to-week typical variation, not instrument reliability.**
   It includes genuine biological fluctuation over up to 10 days. Same-session
   repeat-trial TE would be considerably smaller. What is reported is the right
   denominator for *weekly monitoring decisions* — which is the use case — but
   it should not be quoted as the reliability of the force plate.

2. **The 0.2 × SD convention is harsh in a homogeneous population.** D1
   football athletes within a position band are similar to each other, so the
   between-athlete SD is small, so the SWC is small. This is a known limitation
   of the convention in elite samples rather than a property of these metrics
   specifically.

Both caveats push in the same direction: the ratios above are pessimistic. The
practical conclusion survives anyway.

## What follows operationally

- **Do not act on a single athlete's single-week change.** In every metric, a
  one-week move is dominated by noise. This is the most important line in this
  document.
- **Trends across several tests are the usable unit**, which is an argument for
  denser, more regular testing rather than less. See
  `camp_2026_testing_ask.md`.
- **Stop defaulting to RSI-modified.** It is the field's habitual readiness
  metric and it carries **more than twice** the week-to-week noise of Peak
  Power / BM (8.8% vs 3.8%) in this population.
- **Peak Power / BM is the best headline metric**, on the reliability /
  responsiveness trade-off rather than on either alone. Concentric Impulse is
  quieter (TE 2.9%, ratio 0.99) but essentially inert — its mean Monday →
  Thursday change is +0.06%, so it is stable precisely because nothing moves
  it. Peak Power / BM is second-quietest and second-most responsive (+0.90%).

## IMTP: same analysis, and the cadence implication

`python -m src.research.measurement --imtp --timescale`

| IMTP metric | TE % | SWC/TE |
|---|---|---|
| Peak Vertical Force | 8.8 | 0.39 |
| Peak Vertical Force / BM | 8.9 | 0.35 |
| RFD − 200ms | 23.8 | 0.23 |
| RFD − 100ms | 36.6 | 0.21 |

**The RFD metrics are not usable at any cadence.** 24–37% week-to-week noise
means a change would have to be enormous before it carried information.

### How fast does each quality actually change?

For every within-athlete pair of tests, the spread of percent change against
the gap between them. Pure noise stays flat as the gap widens; a developing
quality spreads out.

| Gap | IMTP Peak Force / BM | CMJ Peak Power / BM |
|---|---|---|
| 0–10 days | 13.2% | 6.6% |
| 10–25 days | 14.9% | 6.7% |
| 25–50 days | 16.5% | 6.8% |
| 50–100 days | 16.4% | 7.6% |
| 100–200 days | 17.3% | 8.0% |

Because noise and real drift add in quadrature, they separate:

- **IMTP: noise floor 13.2%, real change accumulated over 3–6 months ≈ 11.1%.**
  Half a season of genuine strength change is *smaller than one week of
  measurement noise.*
- **CMJ: noise floor 6.6%** — half the IMTP figure — and it is the measure
  that responds within a week.

### What follows

Maximal strength is a slow-adapting quality and the data agrees with the
physiology. **A weekly IMTP is sampling roughly ten times faster than the
thing it measures changes.** Four well-spaced tests per season (camp start,
camp end, mid-season, season end) preserve every meaningful comparison,
because those are all month-plus intervals.

This matters operationally because IMTP and CMJ compete for the same slot: of
2,029 IMTP athlete-days in 2023–25, exactly **one** also has a CMJ. Monday is
IMTP, Thursday is CMJ, and that is precisely why only 20% of athlete-weeks
have the paired CMJ needed to see what a training week did.

**Boundary of this claim:** it concerns measurement value only. If the IMTP
functions as a training or priming stimulus, that is a separate justification
this analysis does not touch and should not be used to override.

## A methods finding worth publishing separately

While designing the companion heterogeneity analysis we found that the standard
approach to testing whether athletes differ in their response — fit a slope per
athlete, then test the spread of those slopes with Cochran's Q against a
chi-square reference — **rejects the null 90.7% of the time when nothing is
happening**, at the sample sizes normal in this field (8–12 observations per
athlete).

The cause is that per-athlete slope standard errors are estimated from as few
as one residual degree of freedom, which breaks the chi-square approximation.
The null Q 95th percentile by simulation is **1052** against **82.6** by
chi-square.

On our real data the invalid test reports p = 0.047, I² = 24% — a publishable-
looking individual-response finding. The bootstrap-calibrated p-value is
**0.936**.

Individual-response claims are currently fashionable in applied sport science
and are frequently made at exactly these sample sizes. This is a cheap,
demonstrable, and directly useful correction. Implementation and calibration
evidence are in `src/research/simulate_power.py` and
`docs/practice_load_heterogeneity_design.md`.

## Honest positioning

CMJ reliability and SWC work exists in the literature; this is not a new
method. What is defensible as novel here is the scale (5,930 retest pairs per
metric), the D1 football population, the head-to-head ranking of ten metrics
under one consistent protocol, and — most of all — the demonstration that the
standard individual-response test is invalid at the sample sizes the field
actually uses.

in the training week, so pooling them would charge real weekly rhythm to
measurement noise and overstate TE.

## Results

| Metric | TE % | SWC/TE | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concentric Impulse | 2.9 | 0.99 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Peak Power / BM | 3.8 | 0.78 | cannot resolve SWC |
| P1 Concentric Impulse | 4.8 | 0.69 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Jump Height (Imp-Mom) | 5.7 | 0.63 | cannot resolve SWC |
| P2 Concentric Impulse | 6.3 | 0.57 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Concentric Impulse-100ms | 8.4 | 0.50 | cannot resolve SWC |
| **RSI-modified** | **8.8** | **0.48** | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Duration | 6.6 | 0.42 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Deceleration RFD / BM | 18.4 | 0.42 | cannot resolve SWC |
| Eccentric Peak Power / BM | 13.4 | 0.34 | cannot resolve SWC |

**None of the ten metrics resolves the smallest worthwhile change at
individual, week-to-week resolution.**

## Two caveats, both of which make this less damning than it reads

1. **TE here is week-to-week typical variation, not instrument reliability.**
   It includes genuine biological fluctuation over up to 10 days. Same-session
   repeat-trial TE would be considerably smaller. What is reported is the right
   denominator for *weekly monitoring decisions* — which is the use case — but
   it should not be quoted as the reliability of the force plate.

2. **The 0.2 × SD convention is harsh in a homogeneous population.** D1
   football athletes within a position band are similar to each other, so the
   between-athlete SD is small, so the SWC is small. This is a known limitation
   of the convention in elite samples rather than a property of these metrics
   specifically.

Both caveats push in the same direction: the ratios above are pessimistic. The
practical conclusion survives anyway.

## What follows operationally

- **Do not act on a single athlete's single-week change.** In every metric, a
  one-week move is dominated by noise. This is the most important line in this
  document.
- **Trends across several tests are the usable unit**, which is an argument for
  denser, more regular testing rather than less. See
  `camp_2026_testing_ask.md`.
- **Stop defaulting to RSI-modified.** It is the field's habitual readiness
  metric and it carries **more than twice** the week-to-week noise of Peak
  Power / BM (8.8% vs 3.8%) in this population.
- **Peak Power / BM is the best headline metric**, on the reliability /
  responsiveness trade-off rather than on either alone. Concentric Impulse is
  quieter (TE 2.9%, ratio 0.99) but essentially inert — its mean Monday →
  Thursday change is +0.06%, so it is stable precisely because nothing moves
  it. Peak Power / BM is second-quietest and second-most responsive (+0.90%).

## IMTP: same analysis, and the cadence implication

`python -m src.research.measurement --imtp --timescale`

| IMTP metric | TE % | SWC/TE |
|---|---|---|
| Peak Vertical Force | 8.8 | 0.39 |
| Peak Vertical Force / BM | 8.9 | 0.35 |
| RFD − 200ms | 23.8 | 0.23 |
| RFD − 100ms | 36.6 | 0.21 |

**The RFD metrics are not usable at any cadence.** 24–37% week-to-week noise
means a change would have to be enormous before it carried information.

### How fast does each quality actually change?

For every within-athlete pair of tests, the spread of percent change against
the gap between them. Pure noise stays flat as the gap widens; a developing
quality spreads out.

| Gap | IMTP Peak Force / BM | CMJ Peak Power / BM |
|---|---|---|
| 0–10 days | 13.2% | 6.6% |
| 10–25 days | 14.9% | 6.7% |
| 25–50 days | 16.5% | 6.8% |
| 50–100 days | 16.4% | 7.6% |
| 100–200 days | 17.3% | 8.0% |

Because noise and real drift add in quadrature, they separate:

- **IMTP: noise floor 13.2%, real change accumulated over 3–6 months ≈ 11.1%.**
  Half a season of genuine strength change is *smaller than one week of
  measurement noise.*
- **CMJ: noise floor 6.6%** — half the IMTP figure — and it is the measure
  that responds within a week.

### What follows

Maximal strength is a slow-adapting quality and the data agrees with the
physiology. **A weekly IMTP is sampling roughly ten times faster than the
thing it measures changes.** Four well-spaced tests per season (camp start,
camp end, mid-season, season end) preserve every meaningful comparison,
because those are all month-plus intervals.

This matters operationally because IMTP and CMJ compete for the same slot: of
2,029 IMTP athlete-days in 2023–25, exactly **one** also has a CMJ. Monday is
IMTP, Thursday is CMJ, and that is precisely why only 20% of athlete-weeks
have the paired CMJ needed to see what a training week did.

**Boundary of this claim:** it concerns measurement value only. If the IMTP
functions as a training or priming stimulus, that is a separate justification
this analysis does not touch and should not be used to override.

## A methods finding worth publishing separately

While designing the companion heterogeneity analysis we found that the standard
approach to testing whether athletes differ in their response — fit a slope per
athlete, then test the spread of those slopes with Cochran's Q against a
chi-square reference — **rejects the null 90.7% of the time when nothing is
happening**, at the sample sizes normal in this field (8–12 observations per
athlete).

The cause is that per-athlete slope standard errors are estimated from as few
as one residual degree of freedom, which breaks the chi-square approximation.
The null Q 95th percentile by simulation is **1052** against **82.6** by
chi-square.

On our real data the invalid test reports p = 0.047, I² = 24% — a publishable-
looking individual-response finding. The bootstrap-calibrated p-value is
**0.936**.

Individual-response claims are currently fashionable in applied sport science
and are frequently made at exactly these sample sizes. This is a cheap,
demonstrable, and directly useful correction. Implementation and calibration
evidence are in `src/research/simulate_power.py` and
`docs/practice_load_heterogeneity_design.md`.

## Honest positioning

CMJ reliability and SWC work exists in the literature; this is not a new
method. What is defensible as novel here is the scale (5,930 retest pairs per
metric), the D1 football population, the head-to-head ranking of ten metrics
under one consistent protocol, and — most of all — the demonstration that the
standard individual-response test is invalid at the sample sizes the field
actually uses.

# Peaking and tapering in an in-season college football schedule

## 1. The question

How should we peak and taper in season? It splits into the game week as a small taper, how long qualities last unexposed, game-week readiness, and game-free windows (byes, camp to week 1, postseason).

The sources answer a different question: every peaking model in the library comes from individual-event sports (kayak, swimming, track and field). **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract): taper research does not yet guide a league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5): a season-long peak is unrealistic. No meta-analysed study tested whether adaptations peaked when predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog|Afonso 2019]], pp. 1, 4). So: hold readiness weekly, and peak on purpose only in game-free windows. **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14):** "in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of November as you get closer to the postseason." Inference: in the sources' terms, that is readiness held high every week, with November and the postseason as the priority window and a deliberate peak only where a game-free gap allows one.

## 2. Bottom line

1. Every game week keeps one heavy lower-body session, load high, sets cut [supported direction; the tested minimum, not Issurin's two-session template; no football trial], and one planned max-velocity exposure [contested in the literature; Eric: Issurin "drives ... sprinting recommendations in season" (interview Q16)]. Eric's week already has one heavy lift (Monday) plus a lighter Wednesday lift (interview Q15). Inference: prioritize positions that rarely reach top speed in games.
2. **Eric's week (interview 2026-09-28, Q15):** Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 h before a Saturday kickoff. This is the sources' early-heavy, late-light shape [Issurin (rugby league) and one D-I program; descriptive only]. Rev 2 inferred about 48 h from the last heavy session to kickoff, from [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms|Verkhoshansky's]] [supported] 48 h recovery after high-CNS work (printed p. 15) and Pritchard 2015's 2 to 4 days of cessation before a strength peak. Inference: Eric's 72 h (3 days) sits inside Pritchard's range and is longer than the rev 2 guess; untested in football. Tension: the Monday heavy lift falls about 48 h post-game, inside the window where Norris 2019 and Cosio 2026 report fast-force and hamstring deficits (section 4).
3. Read readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, FT:CT), no arm swing, against each player's norm, not jump height alone or ACWR. They are noisier, so set thresholds from each player's typical error. [supported direction; small football samples] **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a):** the read is on Wednesdays, with individualized thresholds: "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." Inference: this matches the sources' direction. Wednesday is about 96 h post-game, after the Monday lift and Tuesday practice, so it reads the accumulated week, not game recovery alone.
4. **Eric's position (interview 2026-09-28, Q16):** speed fades first, per Issurin, and that drives in-season sprint recommendations. Inference: by that rule, max-velocity exposure recurs within Issurin's 5 ± 3 day window (PDF p. 35). The literature stays split [contested: Issurin and, loosely, Saldanha 2026 for speed first; Mujika and Padilla 2000, Ross and Leveritt 2001 and Bosquet 2013 against]. Inference: Mujika and Padilla 2000 (VO2max falls within 4 weeks) still argues for some aerobic and repeat-effort work each week; heavy practice may already supply it, which our GPS could check.
5. Save a real taper (about 1 to 3 weeks, volume down 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football] Eric names the postseason as the priority window (Q14) but did not say whether it gets a distinct taper.

## 3. Where the sources agree

**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive week cuts volume, keeps frequency and raises the max-speed share ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 105). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): volume down 60 to 90%, frequency down at most 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies, sports not listed in the abstract, mostly endurance per the evidence file): 2 weeks, volume down 41 to 60%. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; 11 strength-trained men, 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut): tapers did not differ significantly; only the higher-intensity one showed small effect-size gains in IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT.

**Strength holds on a small dose.** Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer, says team-sport players hold strength 14 to 16 weeks ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109; secondhand). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; pro soccer, n = 7 per group): one session a week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one every two weeks lost both; jump height did not change in either group. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly non-athletes): one set per exercise per week held strength up to 32 weeks at kept load; too thin for athlete advice, the authors say.

**Heavy early, light late.** For a Sunday game, Issurin (citing Baker 2001, rugby league) lifts Tuesday and Wednesday mornings, holds the key practice ("substantial or big" load) Thursday afternoon, and restricts only the pre-game session ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: for Saturday, lifts move to Monday and Tuesday, key practice to Wednesday. **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (31 D-I players, one program, PDF p. 6): late-season Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a planned duration cut; Thursday did not change.

**Strategy metrics beat output.** Jump height fell only slightly by 24 h while RSImod and FT:CT stayed down ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football|Lewis]], pp. 96-97; n = 5). At 72 h, flight time moved -0.7% and FT:CT -7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue|Gathercole 2015]], p. 7; n = 8). The cost is noise: several phase and RFD variables failed reliability ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division|Heishman 2020]], pp. 5-12). ACWR did no better than an intercept-only model ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor|Impellizzeri 2020]], pp. 4-5).

## 4. Where they disagree

**Heaviest practice day, and the post-game window.** Issurin's key practice is late (Wednesday if shifted for Saturday, Inference). **External:** Wellman's program planned Tuesday as its highest practice (PDF p. 6); Lewis (PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday closest to game demands for linemen. Both sit in the post-game window: after AFL matches, IMTP RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down 17.8% at 72 h and 16.9% at 96 h, CV 16.4% ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th|Norris 2019]], p. 2); after soccer, hamstring RTD and sprint were impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a|Cosio 2026]], p. 8; n = 9, no control). After Saturday, Monday is about 48 h, Tuesday 72, Wednesday 96. **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q15):** heavy lift Monday (about 48 h), heavy practice Tuesday and Wednesday (about 72 and 96 h), a lighter lift Wednesday. Inference: shifted for Saturday, Issurin lifts twice (Monday and Tuesday); Eric's week has one heavy lift and one lighter one. Tension, not a verdict: the Monday heavy lift and Tuesday practice sit inside the window where Norris 2019 (AFL) reports RFD still down at 72 and 96 h and Cosio 2026 (soccer, n = 9, no control) reports hamstring RTD and sprint impaired at 72 h. Neither tested lifting inside that window, and Issurin loads incompletely recovered players by design. Still unresolved: does the Monday lift cost Saturday anything? Settle with our CMJ and sprint data by hours post-game, including a Monday read.

**Which quality goes first (D-6).** Issurin: speed (5 ± 3 days) before aerobic and strength (30 ± 5), no sample ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability|Issurin residuals]] [contested], PDF p. 35). **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic first, speed last. **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 (abstract): within 4 weeks, trained athletes lose VO2max fast, strength little. Inference: sides with class 4. **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-pro soccer players, uncontrolled): after 5 days off, repeated-sprint time and RAST peak velocity worsened; jump and hip adductor and abductor strength held. Inference: leans toward Issurin, though RAST is not a max-velocity test. Against: **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (PDF p. 17): short-sprint detraining is "less severe than may have been reasonably anticipated". **External:** Bosquet et al. 2013 (abstract; 103 studies): cessation cut maximal power least. **External:** Ronnestad (above) kept sprint without max-velocity work. The residual entry notes these may measure cessation versus a retention dose; Issurin calls residual-only design "extremely rigid and inflexible" ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks|Issurin mini-blocks]] [supported], PDF p. 127). **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16):** "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." So for Eric the conflict is settled in Issurin's favour, against his own class-4 slide (p. 47). The library entry keeps its [contested] tag, because the evidence above is unchanged. Settle for our athletes with our data around byes and winter break.

**Lifting near competition (D-5, D-7).** Platonov and Fesenko say it hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera say it keeps force ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract): 2 to 4 days of training cessation looks optimal for peak strength. Inference: football never stops training, so this only bounds the last lift; the shifted Issurin week puts it 4 days out. Eric's last lift (the lighter Wednesday one) ends 72 h, 3 days, out (interview Q15).

**Maintain or build.** **External:** Ronnestad and Spiering (above) maintain on one session; Issurin uses two. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract, partly garbled; freshmen, n = 14 per group, 2 sessions a week): linear training raised 1RM squat 13.8 ± 7.4 kg, nonlinear did not. Inference: building may suit low-snap freshmen.

**Timing models.** [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle|Bompa]] [supported], [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation|Verkhoshansky]] [contested] and [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept|Evans]] [untested] disagree on whether adaptation timing is predictable. Inference: mental models, not a clock.

## 5. What transfers and what does not

**Transfers:** the two-mini-block week as a template, cutting volume not intensity, CMJ strategy metrics. Body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% at stable mass over 2 weeks ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription|Issurin realization]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; triathletes, n = 16, no significance test).

**Does not transfer:** single-peak prescriptions (1 to 3 week realization, kayak dosages, 4 to 12 week delayed gains per Siff and Verkhoshansky, cited by [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching|Bompa]] [supported], and the 3% taper gain in **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003) assume one target event.

**The exception, a bowl.** **External:** Marrier et al. 2017 (abstract; 10 rugby sevens players, 3-week taper): 70 to 80% of peaks fell in the first 2 weeks. **External:** Vachon et al. 2021 (abstract; 14 team-sport studies): moderate gains in power, change of direction and VO2max; no best strategy. **External:** Haugen et al. 2019 (PDF p. 11): 2 to 3 weeks for strength and power sports; smaller gains in sprinters. Fitz-Clarke 1991 finds usual tapers "may be too rigorous and short" ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing|Verkhoshansky taper]] [supported], printed pp. 88-89). Inference: 1 to 3 weeks, speed and heavy lifting kept, not judged by sprint times alone.

## 6. What none of them covers

- **Bye weeks.** **External:** Peterson (grey literature, unverified year; 108 D-I players) found a group x time interaction on a CMJ stretch-shortening factor: the gap between big and skill or mid-size players widened after the bye and persisted 24 h after the next game (PDF p. 52, Table 6). Within-group change is not tested there. Inference: dose byes by position and keep a speed or repeated-sprint exposure, given Saldanha. **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q17):** byes have three practice days, extra rest and recovery, practices "slightly on the higher-volume side compared with a game week", "a recovery focus, along with a speed and strength top-up", and players with few snaps "will probably practice harder that week". Inference: this already doses by playing time, not position; Peterson's split was by position group, so the two do not map one to one.
- **Short weeks, camp to week 1, position groups, low-snap players.** Only descriptive or off-population data: [[research-papers/galiano-2026-more-matches-less-time-how-load-ratios-reveal-gaps-between-training-and-competition-in-foo|Galiano 2026]], [[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching|Claudino 2016]], [[research-papers/merrigan-2022-comparisons-of-countermovement-jump-force-time-characteristics-among-national-collegiate-a|Merrigan 2022]], [[research-papers/lever-2026-game-exposure-shapes-intensity-and-performance-in-division-i-college-football|Lever 2026]], and [[research-papers/aychman-2026-multimodal-indicators-of-non-functional-overreaching-in-ncaa-division-i-american-football|Aychman 2026]] (non-starters recovered worse on lower load; one program, exploratory, pp. 1, 9).
- **Postseason.** Eric names November and the postseason as the priority window (interview Q14). Bowl structure is Inference from kayak calendars; after a long layoff, rebuild contact over 3 to 4 weeks ([[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports|Stokes 2020]], p. 7; expert opinion).
- **Season-long detraining.** Only the 14 to 16 week figure and Hoffman 2003; nothing on starters' speed.

Would fill: Bompa Ch 7, Issurin Ch 4; others in the evidence map, Gaps.

## 7. Eric's baseline

- **Eric's baseline:** daily CMJ mRSI is the readiness marker, "objective, consistent, and actionable" (SportSmith piece); athletes gamed wellness surveys. Inference: matches section 3 and [[research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective|McCall 2023]].
- **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a):** the mRSI read is on Wednesdays, against individualized thresholds (percent change from baseline or a rolling average; SD and SWC for signal versus noise). Inference: matches bottom line 3.
- **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic is lost fastest, speed slowest; that order sets re-exposure. **Superseded by Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16):** he sides with Issurin, speed fades first.
- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** speed every 5 days, aerobic and strength every 30 (class-1 p. 27). These are Issurin's Table 1.6 reproduced in the slides (week1-lecture p. 66), not independent support, and class-1 also says aerobic is gained and lost quickly (pp. 25, 28). Inference: with Q16, the speed half reads as Eric's; the aerobic and strength halves were not asked.
- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** "maintain intensity, reduce volume", a strength retention dose, a waved week (class-1 pp. 17-25; class-8 p. 21). Agrees with section 3. Not claimed in the interview; Eric does not have the in-season sets and reps (Q18).
- **Eric's baseline (class-4 slides, pp. 34, 39), claimed in the interview (Q1):** conditioning targets alactic and aerobic capacity. Inference: fits the 1:7 ratio in 2004 D-I games ([[research-papers/iosia-2008-analysis-of-exercise-to-rest-ratios-during-division-ia-televised-football-competition|Iosia 2008]]).
- **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14, Q15, Q17):** peak every Saturday, November and the postseason first; the week and the byes as in bottom line 2 and section 6. Inference: agrees with section 3 on early-heavy, late-light; the higher-volume bye is closer to a loading week than a taper; the Monday lift sits in tension with the post-game recovery data in section 4.

## 8. Eric's answers (interview 2026-09-28)

The rev 2 questions, answered in `docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`.

1. **What "peak" means (Q14).** Every Saturday, and above all through November into the postseason: "That's when players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs."
2. **Where the heavy work sits (Q15).** Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 h before kickoff. He did not say whether heavy work should wait until Wednesday; the week as run does not. The section 4 tension stays open.
3. **Which quality fades first (Q16).** "I believe Issurin." Class-4 p. 47 is superseded for Eric. The course in-season rules ("maintain intensity, reduce volume") were not claimed, and the in-season sets and reps are not available (Q18).
4. **Bye weeks (Q17).** Three practices, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, harder for low-snap players. Inference: dosed by snaps, not by position.
5. **mRSI rule (Q2, Q2a).** Wednesdays, individualized thresholds: "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." No numeric trigger was given, and no separate linemen or low-snap thresholds beyond individualization.
6. **A distinct postseason taper.** Not answered directly. Q14 names the postseason as the priority window only.

Still open for Eric: whether the postseason gets its own 1 to 3 week taper; the in-season strength dose (Q18); whether the Monday heavy lift at about 48 h post-game is worth checking against a Monday CMJ read.

## 9. Sources used

# Peaking and tapering in an in-season college football schedule

## 1. The question

How should we peak and taper in season? It splits into the game week as a small taper, how long qualities last unexposed, game-week readiness, and game-free windows (byes, camp to week 1, postseason).

The sources answer a different question: every peaking model in the library comes from individual-event sports (kayak, swimming, track and field). **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract): taper research does not yet guide a league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5): a season-long peak is unrealistic. No meta-analysed study tested whether adaptations peaked when predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog|Afonso 2019]], pp. 1, 4). So: hold readiness weekly, and peak on purpose only in game-free windows. **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14):** "in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of November as you get closer to the postseason." Inference: in the sources' terms, that is readiness held high every week, with November and the postseason as the priority window and a deliberate peak only where a game-free gap allows one.

## 2. Bottom line

1. Every game week keeps one heavy lower-body session, load high, sets cut [supported direction; the tested minimum, not Issurin's two-session template; no football trial], and one planned max-velocity exposure [contested in the literature; Eric: Issurin "drives ... sprinting recommendations in season" (interview Q16)]. Eric's week already has one heavy lift (Monday) plus a lighter Wednesday lift (interview Q15). Inference: prioritize positions that rarely reach top speed in games.
2. **Eric's week (interview 2026-09-28, Q15):** Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 h before a Saturday kickoff. This is the sources' early-heavy, late-light shape [Issurin (rugby league) and one D-I program; descriptive only]. Rev 2 inferred about 48 h from the last heavy session to kickoff, from [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms|Verkhoshansky's]] [supported] 48 h recovery after high-CNS work (printed p. 15) and Pritchard 2015's 2 to 4 days of cessation before a strength peak. Inference: Eric's 72 h (3 days) sits inside Pritchard's range and is longer than the rev 2 guess; untested in football. Tension: the Monday heavy lift falls about 48 h post-game, inside the window where Norris 2019 and Cosio 2026 report fast-force and hamstring deficits (section 4).
3. Read readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, FT:CT), no arm swing, against each player's norm, not jump height alone or ACWR. They are noisier, so set thresholds from each player's typical error. [supported direction; small football samples] **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a):** the read is on Wednesdays, with individualized thresholds: "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." Inference: this matches the sources' direction. Wednesday is about 96 h post-game, after the Monday lift and Tuesday practice, so it reads the accumulated week, not game recovery alone.
4. **Eric's position (interview 2026-09-28, Q16):** speed fades first, per Issurin, and that drives in-season sprint recommendations. Inference: by that rule, max-velocity exposure recurs within Issurin's 5 ± 3 day window (PDF p. 35). The literature stays split [contested: Issurin and, loosely, Saldanha 2026 for speed first; Mujika and Padilla 2000, Ross and Leveritt 2001 and Bosquet 2013 against]. Inference: Mujika and Padilla 2000 (VO2max falls within 4 weeks) still argues for some aerobic and repeat-effort work each week; heavy practice may already supply it, which our GPS could check.
5. Save a real taper (about 1 to 3 weeks, volume down 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football] Eric names the postseason as the priority window (Q14) but did not say whether it gets a distinct taper.

## 3. Where the sources agree

**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive week cuts volume, keeps frequency and raises the max-speed share ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 105). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): volume down 60 to 90%, frequency down at most 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies, sports not listed in the abstract, mostly endurance per the evidence file): 2 weeks, volume down 41 to 60%. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; 11 strength-trained men, 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut): tapers did not differ significantly; only the higher-intensity one showed small effect-size gains in IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT.

**Strength holds on a small dose.** Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer, says team-sport players hold strength 14 to 16 weeks ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109; secondhand). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; pro soccer, n = 7 per group): one session a week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one every two weeks lost both; jump height did not change in either group. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly non-athletes): one set per exercise per week held strength up to 32 weeks at kept load; too thin for athlete advice, the authors say.

**Heavy early, light late.** For a Sunday game, Issurin (citing Baker 2001, rugby league) lifts Tuesday and Wednesday mornings, holds the key practice ("substantial or big" load) Thursday afternoon, and restricts only the pre-game session ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle|Issurin in-season]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: for Saturday, lifts move to Monday and Tuesday, key practice to Wednesday. **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (31 D-I players, one program, PDF p. 6): late-season Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a planned duration cut; Thursday did not change.

**Strategy metrics beat output.** Jump height fell only slightly by 24 h while RSImod and FT:CT stayed down ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football|Lewis]], pp. 96-97; n = 5). At 72 h, flight time moved -0.7% and FT:CT -7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue|Gathercole 2015]], p. 7; n = 8). The cost is noise: several phase and RFD variables failed reliability ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division|Heishman 2020]], pp. 5-12). ACWR did no better than an intercept-only model ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor|Impellizzeri 2020]], pp. 4-5).

## 4. Where they disagree

**Heaviest practice day, and the post-game window.** Issurin's key practice is late (Wednesday if shifted for Saturday, Inference). **External:** Wellman's program planned Tuesday as its highest practice (PDF p. 6); Lewis (PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday closest to game demands for linemen. Both sit in the post-game window: after AFL matches, IMTP RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down 17.8% at 72 h and 16.9% at 96 h, CV 16.4% ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th|Norris 2019]], p. 2); after soccer, hamstring RTD and sprint were impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a|Cosio 2026]], p. 8; n = 9, no control). After Saturday, Monday is about 48 h, Tuesday 72, Wednesday 96. **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q15):** heavy lift Monday (about 48 h), heavy practice Tuesday and Wednesday (about 72 and 96 h), a lighter lift Wednesday. Inference: shifted for Saturday, Issurin lifts twice (Monday and Tuesday); Eric's week has one heavy lift and one lighter one. Tension, not a verdict: the Monday heavy lift and Tuesday practice sit inside the window where Norris 2019 (AFL) reports RFD still down at 72 and 96 h and Cosio 2026 (soccer, n = 9, no control) reports hamstring RTD and sprint impaired at 72 h. Neither tested lifting inside that window, and Issurin loads incompletely recovered players by design. Still unresolved: does the Monday lift cost Saturday anything? Settle with our CMJ and sprint data by hours post-game, including a Monday read.

**Which quality goes first (D-6).** Issurin: speed (5 ± 3 days) before aerobic and strength (30 ± 5), no sample ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability|Issurin residuals]] [contested], PDF p. 35). **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic first, speed last. **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 (abstract): within 4 weeks, trained athletes lose VO2max fast, strength little. Inference: sides with class 4. **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-pro soccer players, uncontrolled): after 5 days off, repeated-sprint time and RAST peak velocity worsened; jump and hip adductor and abductor strength held. Inference: leans toward Issurin, though RAST is not a max-velocity test. Against: **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (PDF p. 17): short-sprint detraining is "less severe than may have been reasonably anticipated". **External:** Bosquet et al. 2013 (abstract; 103 studies): cessation cut maximal power least. **External:** Ronnestad (above) kept sprint without max-velocity work. The residual entry notes these may measure cessation versus a retention dose; Issurin calls residual-only design "extremely rigid and inflexible" ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks|Issurin mini-blocks]] [supported], PDF p. 127). **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16):** "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." So for Eric the conflict is settled in Issurin's favour, against his own class-4 slide (p. 47). The library entry keeps its [contested] tag, because the evidence above is unchanged. Settle for our athletes with our data around byes and winter break.

**Lifting near competition (D-5, D-7).** Platonov and Fesenko say it hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera say it keeps force ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning|Issurin pre-competitive]] [supported], PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract): 2 to 4 days of training cessation looks optimal for peak strength. Inference: football never stops training, so this only bounds the last lift; the shifted Issurin week puts it 4 days out. Eric's last lift (the lighter Wednesday one) ends 72 h, 3 days, out (interview Q15).

**Maintain or build.** **External:** Ronnestad and Spiering (above) maintain on one session; Issurin uses two. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract, partly garbled; freshmen, n = 14 per group, 2 sessions a week): linear training raised 1RM squat 13.8 ± 7.4 kg, nonlinear did not. Inference: building may suit low-snap freshmen.

**Timing models.** [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle|Bompa]] [supported], [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation|Verkhoshansky]] [contested] and [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept|Evans]] [untested] disagree on whether adaptation timing is predictable. Inference: mental models, not a clock.

## 5. What transfers and what does not

**Transfers:** the two-mini-block week as a template, cutting volume not intensity, CMJ strategy metrics. Body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% at stable mass over 2 weeks ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription|Issurin realization]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; triathletes, n = 16, no significance test).

**Does not transfer:** single-peak prescriptions (1 to 3 week realization, kayak dosages, 4 to 12 week delayed gains per Siff and Verkhoshansky, cited by [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching|Bompa]] [supported], and the 3% taper gain in **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003) assume one target event.

**The exception, a bowl.** **External:** Marrier et al. 2017 (abstract; 10 rugby sevens players, 3-week taper): 70 to 80% of peaks fell in the first 2 weeks. **External:** Vachon et al. 2021 (abstract; 14 team-sport studies): moderate gains in power, change of direction and VO2max; no best strategy. **External:** Haugen et al. 2019 (PDF p. 11): 2 to 3 weeks for strength and power sports; smaller gains in sprinters. Fitz-Clarke 1991 finds usual tapers "may be too rigorous and short" ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing|Verkhoshansky taper]] [supported], printed pp. 88-89). Inference: 1 to 3 weeks, speed and heavy lifting kept, not judged by sprint times alone.

## 6. What none of them covers

- **Bye weeks.** **External:** Peterson (grey literature, unverified year; 108 D-I players) found a group x time interaction on a CMJ stretch-shortening factor: the gap between big and skill or mid-size players widened after the bye and persisted 24 h after the next game (PDF p. 52, Table 6). Within-group change is not tested there. Inference: dose byes by position and keep a speed or repeated-sprint exposure, given Saldanha. **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q17):** byes have three practice days, extra rest and recovery, practices "slightly on the higher-volume side compared with a game week", "a recovery focus, along with a speed and strength top-up", and players with few snaps "will probably practice harder that week". Inference: this already doses by playing time, not position; Peterson's split was by position group, so the two do not map one to one.
- **Short weeks, camp to week 1, position groups, low-snap players.** Only descriptive or off-population data: [[research-papers/galiano-2026-more-matches-less-time-how-load-ratios-reveal-gaps-between-training-and-competition-in-foo|Galiano 2026]], [[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching|Claudino 2016]], [[research-papers/merrigan-2022-comparisons-of-countermovement-jump-force-time-characteristics-among-national-collegiate-a|Merrigan 2022]], [[research-papers/lever-2026-game-exposure-shapes-intensity-and-performance-in-division-i-college-football|Lever 2026]], and [[research-papers/aychman-2026-multimodal-indicators-of-non-functional-overreaching-in-ncaa-division-i-american-football|Aychman 2026]] (non-starters recovered worse on lower load; one program, exploratory, pp. 1, 9).
- **Postseason.** Eric names November and the postseason as the priority window (interview Q14). Bowl structure is Inference from kayak calendars; after a long layoff, rebuild contact over 3 to 4 weeks ([[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports|Stokes 2020]], p. 7; expert opinion).
- **Season-long detraining.** Only the 14 to 16 week figure and Hoffman 2003; nothing on starters' speed.

Would fill: Bompa Ch 7, Issurin Ch 4; others in the evidence map, Gaps.

## 7. Eric's baseline

- **Eric's baseline:** daily CMJ mRSI is the readiness marker, "objective, consistent, and actionable" (SportSmith piece); athletes gamed wellness surveys. Inference: matches section 3 and [[research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective|McCall 2023]].
- **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a):** the mRSI read is on Wednesdays, against individualized thresholds (percent change from baseline or a rolling average; SD and SWC for signal versus noise). Inference: matches bottom line 3.
- **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic is lost fastest, speed slowest; that order sets re-exposure. **Superseded by Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16):** he sides with Issurin, speed fades first.
- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** speed every 5 days, aerobic and strength every 30 (class-1 p. 27). These are Issurin's Table 1.6 reproduced in the slides (week1-lecture p. 66), not independent support, and class-1 also says aerobic is gained and lost quickly (pp. 25, 28). Inference: with Q16, the speed half reads as Eric's; the aerobic and strength halves were not asked.
- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** "maintain intensity, reduce volume", a strength retention dose, a waved week (class-1 pp. 17-25; class-8 p. 21). Agrees with section 3. Not claimed in the interview; Eric does not have the in-season sets and reps (Q18).
- **Eric's baseline (class-4 slides, pp. 34, 39), claimed in the interview (Q1):** conditioning targets alactic and aerobic capacity. Inference: fits the 1:7 ratio in 2004 D-I games ([[research-papers/iosia-2008-analysis-of-exercise-to-rest-ratios-during-division-ia-televised-football-competition|Iosia 2008]]).
- **Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14, Q15, Q17):** peak every Saturday, November and the postseason first; the week and the byes as in bottom line 2 and section 6. Inference: agrees with section 3 on early-heavy, late-light; the higher-volume bye is closer to a loading week than a taper; the Monday lift sits in tension with the post-game recovery data in section 4.

## 8. Eric's answers (interview 2026-09-28)

The rev 2 questions, answered in `docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`.

1. **What "peak" means (Q14).** Every Saturday, and above all through November into the postseason: "That's when players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs."
2. **Where the heavy work sits (Q15).** Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 h before kickoff. He did not say whether heavy work should wait until Wednesday; the week as run does not. The section 4 tension stays open.
3. **Which quality fades first (Q16).** "I believe Issurin." Class-4 p. 47 is superseded for Eric. The course in-season rules ("maintain intensity, reduce volume") were not claimed, and the in-season sets and reps are not available (Q18).
4. **Bye weeks (Q17).** Three practices, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, harder for low-snap players. Inference: dosed by snaps, not by position.
5. **mRSI rule (Q2, Q2a).** Wednesdays, individualized thresholds: "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." No numeric trigger was given, and no separate linemen or low-snap thresholds beyond individualization.
6. **A distinct postseason taper.** Not answered directly. Q14 names the postseason as the priority window only.

Still open for Eric: whether the postseason gets its own 1 to 3 week taper; the in-season strength dose (Q18); whether the Monday heavy lift at about 48 h post-game is worth checking against a Monday CMJ read.

content.content:
# Readiness moved from RSI-modified to Peak Power / BM

**Decision date:** 2026-07-22

The readiness flag (green / yellow / orange / red) is now computed from
**Peak Power / BM** instead of **RSI-modified**. The gold / purple / white
performance tier is unchanged and still comes from RSI-modified percentiles.

---

## Why

RSI-modified is the noisiest of the metrics we lead with. Measured over the same
5,930 stable retest pairs (consecutive same-weekday tests <= 10 days apart,
2023-25, tails trimmed at 1/99pct):

| Metric | Typical error | Change-score SD |
|---|---|---|
| Peak Power / BM | **3.8%** | **5.40%** |
| RSI-modified | 8.8% | 13.09% |

Peak Power / BM carries less than half the measurement noise. A real drop of a
given size is correspondingly easier to separate from noise. Of the ten CMJ
metrics, Peak Power / BM also has the best signal-to-noise ratio against the
smallest worthwhile change (SWC/TE 0.78 vs 0.48).

## Why the thresholds had to change with it

**This is the part that matters.** Applying the existing RSI-modified ladder
(single-test 30 / 25 / 15) to Peak Power / BM unchanged fires on **0.00% of
noise-only comparisons** — a classifier that never flags anyone. The thresholds
are not a stylistic choice; each one is positioned against the noise of a
specific metric.

noise-only comparisons that would trip it — and the rates are held identical
across both metrics. A "red" therefore means the same thing whichever metric
produced it.

|---|---|---|---|
| Single-test red | 1.30% | >30% | **>12%** |
| Single-test orange | 2.50% | >25% | **>11%** |
| Single-test yellow | 9.80% | >15% | **>7%** |
| Consecutive red | 0.96% | >15% both | **>7% both** |
| Consecutive orange | 3.32% | >10% both | **>5% both** |
| Consecutive yellow | 10.49% | >5% both | **>2.5% both** |

6.7 / 4.6 / 2.3) rounded outward, which is how the RSI-modified ladder was
rounded. They land at roughly 40% of the RSI-modified numbers, exactly what the
5.40% vs 13.09% change-score SD predicts.

recovers 27.7 / 24.0 / 14.7 and 14.7 / 9.8 / 4.9, which is the shipped
30 / 25 / 15 and 15 / 10 / 5 after rounding.

## Effect on the stored history

All 10,730 classified rows were reclassified on 2026-07-22.

| Flag | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| green | 6,924 | 8,576 | +1,652 |
| yellow | 1,232 | 831 | −401 |
| orange | 954 | 490 | −464 |
| red | 1,620 | 833 | −787 |
| **non-green total** | **3,806** | **2,154** | **−43%** |

(">10% -> red") fired on 18.2% of noise-only comparisons, so roughly one red in

before the flags are used operationally. **Fewer flags is not the same as fewer
athletes needing attention**; it means the flags that remain are the ones that
outrun the measurement error.

Readiness falls back to RSI-modified when an athlete has no Peak Power baseline.

test, which has no baseline of any kind and is green by definition.

   calling `resolve_position`, so those tests were dropped without warning. The

   place.

2. **A fresh database and a migrated one would have had different column
   orders.** The new columns were added mid-table in `CREATE TABLE` but
   `ALTER TABLE` appends at the end. They are now declared last so both paths
   produce an identical schema.

- **20,049 rows in `raw_tests` have a blank position** and have always been
  skipped by classification. This predates the switch and is unchanged by it,
  but it is now reported rather than silent. Whether these are legitimately
  excluded needs a look.
- The **gold / purple / white tier still uses RSI-modified.** Ranking athletes on
  a different quality is a strength-and-conditioning judgment, not a measurement
  one, so it was deliberately left alone.

## Reproducing the calibration

```
python -m src.research.measurement          # CMJ typical error table
```

Threshold constants live in `src/classify/engine.py`
(`PEAK_POWER_SINGLE_TEST_THRESHOLDS`, `PEAK_POWER_CONSECUTIVE_THRESHOLDS`).
