# CMJ fatigue metrics: evidence review for the Monday/Wednesday decision tree

**Question.** Which VALD ForceDecks CMJ metrics (2 jumps, hands on hips, lift warm-up, Monday about 48 h post-game and Wednesday about 72 h pre-kickoff) best detect neuromuscular fatigue in NCAA Division I American football players? The answer should be good enough to flag players for practice modification (reported to position coaches) and to modify the Monday and Wednesday lifts.

**Prepared:** 2026-11-05. Zotero first (via `zotero-bridge`), external peer-reviewed sources labelled `[External]`. No athlete-identifiable data.

**How to read the tags.**
- `[Zotero: KEY, p. N]`: page-located in Eric's library. Page numbers are **bridge PDF page indices**, not printed page numbers. For dissertations they differ: Lewis PDF p. 96 = printed p. 78; Peterson PDF p. 89 = printed p. 78.
- `[Zotero: KEY, abstract]`: in the library, but only the abstract or metadata was read.
- `[External]`: not in Zotero; link given.
- `[Baylor]`: the department's own analysis files (2023-25 ForceDecks data, 185 athletes, 5,930 retest pairs per metric).
- Every claim is also labelled **(finding)** for a direct study result, **(synthesis)** for a cross-paper conclusion, or **(interpretation)** for practitioner judgement.

---

## Practical answer

1. **Keep one output metric and one strategy metric. Drop the rest as flags.**
   - Primary output metric: **Peak Power / BM**.
   - Strategy metric: **RSI-modified**, with a much wider, noise-calibrated threshold.
   - Explain-only metrics (shown, never flagged): **jump height (Imp-Mom)**, **contraction time / time to take-off**, **eccentric duration**, **countermovement depth** (also a protocol QC check).
   - Drop as flag inputs: eccentric deceleration RFD, concentric impulse, mean force, and contraction time on its own.
2. **The draft thresholds are not defensible as written.** One % cut (-6.5 / -10) is applied to three metrics whose noise differs by more than 2x.
   - On RSI-mod, Baylor's own data show the -10% RED rule fires on about **18% of noise-only comparisons**.
   - The -6.5% AMBER boundary sits at about half an SD of week-to-week RSI-mod noise, so it would turn roughly **30%** of healthy tests amber.
   - On Peak Power / BM the same numbers land near Baylor's already-calibrated yellow and orange cuts.
   - CT +5-8% sits inside one CV of CT noise.
   - Replace the cuts with the department's false-positive-calibrated ladder (PP/BM: 7 / 11 / 12%; RSI-mod: 15 / 25 / 30%), plus a **two-test rule** (Monday and Wednesday both down), against **weekday-specific baselines**.
3. **Use the mean of the 2 jumps, not the best.** Add a third jump when the two disagree.
4. **The tool is decision support, not a proven intervention.** No trial in any football code shows that CMJ-guided load modification reduces injury or improves game performance. The evidence for detection is moderate. The evidence that acting on a flag helps is close to none.

---

## Q1. Sensitivity versus reliability, metric by metric

### The "outcome vs strategy" point (synthesis)

Fatigue can leave the jump **outcome** (height, power) intact while changing **how** the jump is made (longer contraction and eccentric time, lower FT:CT or RSI-mod).

- Gathercole 2015 (11 male college team-sport athletes, running fatigue protocol, not a match) **(finding)**:
  - At 72 h, flight time changed only -0.7% while FT:CT fell -7.7% and total duration rose 7.6% [Zotero: NAFZ3EN2, p. 7].
  - In the results table, jump height at 72 h was a trivial *increase* (ES +0.18), while FT:CT was a small decrease (ES -0.44) [Zotero: NAFZ3EN2, p. 8].
  - The authors advise adding "variables that reflect the NM strategy used" [Zotero: NAFZ3EN2, p. 2].
- In DI football, CMJ jump height rose significantly by 72 h post-game, while match load slowed the recovery of RSI-mod and time to take-off [External: Talpey et al. 2026] **(finding)**.
- Bishop et al. 2023 conclude that jump height and peak power "may be less sensitive" to fatigue than time-based metrics (time to peak power, FT:CT, which is "essentially the same as RSI_Mod", and time to take-off) [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, pp. 3-4] **(synthesis, narrative review)**.
  - Bishop cites Claudino 2017 as finding ES -0.04 for maximal JH and PP after fatiguing protocols. That is Bishop's reading; the Claudino pages read here do not show it directly.

### Ranking table

How the columns were built:
- **Sensitivity**: literature effect sizes after match or fatigue.
- **Lit. reliability**: inter-session CV / ICC, no arm swing, from Heishman 2020 [Zotero: BAV77QQL, Tables 4, 6, 8, pp. 5-8], DI basketball, ForceDecks.
- **Baylor TE**: week-to-week typical error and SWC/TE [Baylor: `cmj_measurement_properties.md`].

| Rank for this tool | Metric | Sensitivity to fatigue (literature) | Lit. reliability (CV%, ICC) | Baylor TE % (SWC/TE) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Peak Power / BM** | Moderate. PP fell after contact-code matches (SMD -0.80 at 24 h) [External: Hagstrom & Shorter 2018]. Youth AF PP down to 68 h [External: Davis 2021]. Weaker after lab protocols per Bishop [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 3]. | Abs PP 3.7%, ICC 0.96 | **3.8 (0.78)**, best ratio of 10 | **Primary output flag** |
| 2 | **RSI-mod** (Imp-Mom) | High. Large drops 0-24 h after a football lift session (ES -1.24 / -1.05; n = 5) [Zotero: 8XYJQFMV, PDF p. 97]. Match load slowed its recovery in DI football [External: Talpey 2026]. Linked to biomarker strain mid-season [Zotero: GZBHYCNM, abstract]. | 10.4%, ICC 0.85; Mercer 11.7% (mean of 3) [Zotero: QJ2IG6CA, p. 5]; "poor test-retest" [Zotero: 6KR3ZVIW, abstract] | **8.8 (0.48)** | **Strategy flag**, wide threshold only |
| 3 | FT:CT | High; the classic AFL marker: reduced on 60% of in-season occasions, up to -17% [Zotero: IGW9WRQB, p. 1]. Same construct as RSI-mod [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 4]. | 9.3%, ICC 0.78 | not measured | Redundant with RSI-mod; pick one |
| 4 | Jump height (Imp-Mom) | Low-moderate. Can hold or rise while strategy degrades (above). Rugby union meta: small non-significant drops at 24/48 h [Zotero: CNJETVCQ, p. 1]. | 5.4%, ICC 0.94 | 5.7 (0.63) | Context only (it is the numerator of RSI-mod) |
| 5 | Contraction time / time to take-off | Moderate-high. Large duration increases after fatigue [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 4]. Match-load effect in DI football [External: Talpey 2026]. | 8.5%, **ICC 0.61**. TTT "not reliable" in DI football [External: Talpey 2025] | not measured | Explainer, not a flag |
| 6 | Eccentric duration | High acutely (ES 1.91-1.93) [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 4; 8XYJQFMV, PDF p. 97] | 11.7%, **ICC 0.52** | 6.6 (0.42) | Explainer |
| 7 | Countermovement depth | A strategy dimension (its own principal component in DI football) [Zotero: 7KY6KMGR, p. 1]. Depth changes the output metrics [Zotero: K9IX3SMP, abstract]. | (not in Heishman) | not measured | **QC check**: a depth change of more than a few cm invalidates the comparison |
| 8 | Concentric impulse | Low. Baylor mean Mon->Thu change +0.06%, "inert" | 2.7%, ICC 0.98 | 2.9 (0.99) | Drop. Quiet because nothing moves it; absolute value tracks body mass |
| 9 | Ecc. deceleration RFD / impulse | Fell after basketball practice [Zotero: A2Y3BKFY, abstract] | **26.3%**. Mercer RFD 18.5%, decel *impulse* 7.7% [Zotero: QJ2IG6CA, p. 4]. Ecc RFD and impulse unreliable intrasession [Zotero: MUJBA4LK, abstract]. RFD biased across systems [Zotero: 6KR3ZVIW, abstract] | 18.4 (0.42) | Drop RFD. Decel impulse is the only eccentric candidate worth a local test |
| 10 | Mean force (ecc. mean force) | Very low; approximately body weight | 0.8%, ICC 0.995 | not measured | Drop. Reliable because it barely measures anything |

**Rank order agrees (synthesis).** Baylor's noise ranking and the literature's agree closely:
- Concentric impulse is quietest.
- PP next.
- Then JH.
- Then the timing and ratio metrics.
- Eccentric RFD is the worst.

Heishman, Mercer, Merrigan 2024 and Baylor all put RSI-mod among the noisier metrics.

---

## Q2. Are the -6.5% / -10% thresholds defensible?

**Short answer: no, not as one cut across three metrics.** The cuts happen to be roughly right for Peak Power / BM and wrong for RSI-mod. For contraction time they are uncalibrated.

### What a cut costs in false flags (synthesis, computed from Baylor's numbers)

Method:
- Approximate one-sided rate at which a noise-only change exceeds the cut, assuming normal change scores.
- RSI-mod and PP/BM change-score SDs from [Baylor: `readiness_metric_switch.md`]: 13.09% and 5.40%.
- JH change-score SD estimated as TE x sqrt(2) = 8.1%.
- These are approximations. Baylor's empirical figure is the one to trust where it exists.

| Draft cut | RSI-mod | Jump height | PP/BM (for comparison) |
|---|---|---|---|
| AMBER at -6.5% to -7% | about 30% of healthy tests | about 20% | about 10% (near Baylor's calibrated *yellow*, >7%) |
| RED at -10% | about 22% normal approximation; **18.2% empirical** [Baylor] | about 11% | about 3% (between Baylor yellow and orange) |
| CT AMBER +5-8% | Inside one inter-session CV (8.5%, ICC 0.61) [Zotero: BAV77QQL, p. 6] | | |

- **(finding, Baylor)** The old ">10% -> red" RSI-mod rule meant "roughly one red in five was measurement noise". Recalibrating to equal false-positive rates gives RSI-mod 15 / 25 / 30% and PP/BM 7 / 11 / 12% (single test), with consecutive-test cuts of 5 / 10 / 15% and 2.5 / 5 / 7% [Baylor: `readiness_metric_switch.md`].
- **(interpretation)** The Wednesday cuts (-6 / -11%) have no separate evidence base. Noise does not change by weekday. Only the action on a Wednesday flag differs.

### Individual SWC / CV / z-scores vs fixed % cuts

- **(synthesis)** The literature recommends athlete-specific baselines with distribution-based thresholds (SD bands, minimal detectable change), chosen with explicit Type I / Type II trade-offs [Zotero: QQD4DSC4, pp. 1-2].
  - Claudino 2016 autoregulated training with the individual "minimal individual difference" in CMJ height [Zotero: T6EYDYN3, p. 1].
- **(finding, Baylor)** No CMJ metric resolves the 0.2 x between-athlete-SD SWC at individual week-to-week resolution (all SWC/TE < 1) [Baylor: `cmj_measurement_properties.md`].
- **(interpretation)** For *fatigue* detection the right yardstick is noise (TE), not SWC. A flag should mean "this drop is bigger than normal week-to-week variation".
  - Reported post-game and post-fatigue changes are about the same size as one TE. Examples: FT:CT -7.7% [Zotero: NAFZ3EN2, p. 7]; RSI-mod / CMRJ effects d of about 0.5 at 24 h [External: Talpey 2026].
  - So a **single** test can only catch large drops. Repeated or consecutive tests are the usable unit, as the measurement doc concludes.
- **(interpretation, Baylor)** Per-athlete SDs need many tests. At 8-12 observations per athlete, Baylor found the standard individual-response test rejects the null 90.7% of the time under no effect.
  - Practical consequence: use **pooled (position-band) TE** to set thresholds, then express each player's change against his own baseline. Do not trust individual SDs until a player has 10+ same-weekday tests.
- **% cut vs z-score.** A % cut is fine *if* it is derived from that metric's TE. Baylor's ladder is exactly that and is easier for coaches to read than a z-score.

### Rolling vs fixed baselines

- **(finding)** Cormack 2008 compared weekly values with a pre-season baseline. FT:CT reductions against it tracked periods of fatigue across a 22-match AFL season [Zotero: IGW9WRQB, pp. 1, 13].
- **(finding, Baylor)** The shipped readiness baseline is "each athlete's earliest test" [Baylor: `readiness_metric_switch.md`].
  - **(interpretation)** For returning players this anchor can be years old. Training adaptation then hides fatigue, or a strength gain looks like readiness.
- **(finding, Baylor)** Same-weekday pairing is deliberate: Monday and Thursday differ in weekly rhythm, and pooling them overstates TE [Baylor: `cmj_measurement_properties.md`].
- **Recommendation (interpretation).** A **weekday-specific** baseline:
  - Monday is compared with Mondays, Wednesday with Wednesdays.
  - Each is the mean of that player's last 4-6 non-flagged same-weekday tests (rolling).
  - It is re-anchored each fall camp, with a season-start reference kept alongside so slow drift (chronic decline) stays visible.
  - A pure rolling baseline can absorb accumulating fatigue. The camp anchor is the guard against that.

### How many reps: best vs mean of 2

- **(finding)** Meta-analysis of 151 studies: average CMJ height was more sensitive than highest CMJ height for detecting fatigue and supercompensation. All comparisons favoured the average [Zotero: SCL9W3QP, pp. 1, 4].
- **(finding)** In professional basketball, mean of 3 had lower inter-day CV than best-JH trial for 79 of 84 variables. Mean of 3 gave seasonal signal above noise for 77 of 84 variables, against 65 for best-JH and 58 for best-FT:CT [Zotero: QJ2IG6CA, pp. 1, 3].
- **(finding)** Two maximal CMJs on force plates gave acceptable intrasession reliability for most metrics in DI athletes, except RFD, eccentric impulse and stiffness [Zotero: MUJBA4LK, abstract].
- **(finding)** Across a 6-jump clustered protocol (314 athletes), the best output trial most often came on rep 4, not rep 1 or 2 [External: Kruczek et al. 2026, *J Sports Sci*].
  - **(interpretation)** "Best of 2" is a biased sample of the true best. The mean of 2 is the more honest estimate.
- **Recommendation.** Mean of 2. Add a 3rd jump when the two differ in jump height by more than about 5%, or when depth differs visibly.
- **Open question for Baylor:** were the TE figures computed on best or mean trials? The thresholds should be built on the same summary the tool uses.

---

## Q3. American football evidence: post-game time course and in-season monitoring

| Study | Population / design | What it shows | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Talpey et al. 2026, *JSCR* 40(6):682-688 | 29 DI players, 2 games; CMJ and rebound CMJ at -24 h, +24 h, +72 h; dual force plates; GPS PlayerLoad | **(finding)** Rebound-CMJ power, RSI-mod and JH fell at 24 h (d 0.46-0.67), with power recovered by 72 h. CMJ JH *increased* by 72 h. Match load mediated recovery of CMJ RSI-mod (p = 0.004) and time to take-off (p = 0.016). | [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000005386) |
| Talpey et al. 2025, *JSCR* 39(2):200-209 | 46 DI players, 3 days | **(finding)** Most CMJ variables reliable *except time to take-off*. Rebound-phase CVs >10%. | [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000004969) |
| Kraemer et al. 2009; Sterczala et al. 2014 | DI, starters vs DNP; game 9 | **(finding)** CK and myoglobin raised at 18-20 h and back near pre-game by 42-44 h (Monday), with stable hormones. No jump data. | [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e31819306f2), [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000000467) |
| Davis et al. 2021, *JSCR* | 13 *youth* AF players, one game, 7 days | **(finding)** CMJ PP, JH and take-off velocity down up to 68 h; flight time up to 44 h. | [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004011) |
| Lewis (dissertation, 2021) | 5 college AF players, **post-training session, not a game** | **(finding)** FT:CT and RSI-mod large drops at 0 h (ES -1.20 / -1.24) and still at 24 h (-1.08 / -1.05). JH only small at 24 h (-0.27). | [Zotero: 8XYJQFMV, PDF pp. 96-98] |
| Aychman et al. 2026, *Front Physiol* | 39 DI players, 15-week season | **(finding)** Mid-season CMJ declines alongside biomarker changes. Non-starters showed more strain despite lower load. Exploratory, one program. | [Zotero: GZBHYCNM, abstract] |
| Merrigan et al. 2022, *JSCR* | 82 DI players, 2 no-arm-swing CMJs | **(finding)** Linemen have longer propulsive durations and lower RSI-mod than skill players. Four components: explosive transfer (RSI-mod), eccentric loading, countermovement strategy, height/power. | [Zotero: 7KY6KMGR, p. 1] |
| Peterson (dissertation, 2024) | DI football, 4 seasons | **(finding, exploratory)** More than 10% drop in an SSC factor at baseline linked to traumatic lower-extremity injury, OR 6.49 (90% CI 1.22-34.38, p = 0.065). The simpler model fit as well (LRT p = 0.76). No in-season NFOR x week effect. Hypothesis-generating only. | [Zotero: UWCY55NG, PDF pp. 4, 89, 93] |
| Hagstrom & Shorter 2018 | Meta-analysis, contact football codes | **(finding)** CMJ PP down immediately (SMD -0.59) and at 24 h (-0.80). CK up to 48 h. | [External](https://doi.org/10.1080/17461391.2018.1480661) |

**Not found** (Zotero or external search):
- No college or NFL CMJ data at exactly **48 h** post-game. That is the Monday slot. Talpey is 24 and 72 h. Kraemer is CK at 42-44 h.
- No **NFL** post-game CMJ time course.
- Nothing on CMJ at the Wednesday (~96 h post-game) slot.

**(synthesis)** The 48 h status has to be interpolated. Output metrics in college players are mostly back by 72 h, and some overshoot. Strategy metrics recover more slowly and depend on game load. Monday is the slot where a strategy-metric flag is most likely to be real.

**(interpretation)** Football position groups differ enough that thresholds and baselines should be position-band aware [Zotero: 7KY6KMGR, p. 1]. Snap count belongs in the context column [External: Talpey 2026; Zotero: GZBHYCNM, abstract].

---

## Q4. Does CMJ-guided load modification change outcomes?

- **Only controlled trial found (finding).** U17 futsal, 9 vs 9, randomised. Training load autoregulated from mean CMJ height and each player's minimal individual difference. The regulated group overreached more, then rose above baseline after the taper (ES 0.30); controls did not change [Zotero: T6EYDYN3, p. 1].
  - The outcome was the CMJ itself, not game performance or injury.
- **Associations with match output (finding).** Some evidence links CMJ status to on-field output:
  - AFL players flagged "fatigued" by FT:CT had a -5.8% vertical-vector contribution to accelerometer load and less high-speed running [Zotero: QQXUXWCX, PDF p. 4].
  - FT:CT showed a small correlation with coach-rated performance (r = 0.24) [Zotero: IGW9WRQB, p. 1].
- **Against (finding).** In A-League soccer, training-load effects on pre-match FT:CT were "mostly unclear or trivial" [External: Rowell et al. 2018].
  - **(finding, Baylor)** Six attempts to detect a practice-load effect on readiness returned nothing [Baylor: `cmj_measurement_properties.md`].
- **Injury.** Only Peterson's exploratory association (above). Bishop notes peak power did not predict future injury in rugby league or AFL [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 4].
- **Caution (synthesis).** Kruczek et al. 2026 argue that readiness flags get too much decision weight in under-prepared athletes. Repeatedly cutting training for "trivial short-term fluctuations" erodes the capacity the athlete still needs [External: Kruczek, Rebelo, Gabbett, Nowak 2026, *Front Physiol*].
  - **(interpretation)** In football terms: a red on a low-snap player should change *what* he does, not just reduce it.

**(synthesis) Verdict.** The CMJ detects fatigue. There is no evidence that modifying practice or lifts on a CMJ flag improves injury rates or game performance in any football code. Build the tool as decision support, and log every flag with the action taken, so Baylor can later compare flagged-and-modified with flagged-and-not-modified.

---

## Q5. Recommended metric set

| Role | Metric | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary output** | **Peak Power / BM** (mean of 2) | Lowest noise with a usable response in Baylor's data (TE 3.8%, best SWC/TE) [Baylor]. Literature reliability agrees (CV 3.7%, ICC 0.96) [Zotero: BAV77QQL, p. 5]. Sensitive to contact-code matches at 24 h [External: Hagstrom 2018]. Already the department's readiness metric, so the tool and the readiness flag agree. |
| **Strategy 1** | **RSI-mod** (Imp-Mom) | The most fatigue-sensitive metric in football and team-sport data [Zotero: 8XYJQFMV, PDF p. 97; External: Talpey 2026; Zotero: IGW9WRQB, p. 1]. Catches the "height held, timing slowed" pattern. Too noisy for a tight cut (TE 8.8%), so flag only on Baylor's RSI-mod ladder (15 / 25 / 30%) or on two consecutive tests. |
| **Strategy 2 (explain only)** | **Contraction time** (or eccentric duration) | When RSI-mod drops and JH holds, CT says the timing moved. Shown on the report but never flagged alone: ICC 0.61 [Zotero: BAV77QQL, p. 6], TTT unreliable in DI football [External: Talpey 2025]. |
| **QC** | Countermovement depth | A changed depth changes every timing metric [Zotero: K9IX3SMP, abstract; 7KY6KMGR, p. 1]. Re-jump, or mark the test non-comparable. |
| **Drop** | Eccentric deceleration RFD; concentric impulse; mean force; FT:CT as a separate metric; jump height as a separate flag | Unreliable (RFD), inert (impulse), insensitive (mean force), or redundant (FT:CT, JH, which are already inside RSI-mod). |

**Flag logic (interpretation, built on Baylor's calibration):**
- **GREEN**: PP/BM and RSI-mod both within the yellow cut against the same-weekday baseline.
- **AMBER**: PP/BM down more than 7%, *or* RSI-mod down more than 15%, *or* both Monday and Wednesday down by the consecutive cuts (PP/BM 2.5-5%, RSI-mod 5-10%).
- **RED**: PP/BM down more than 11-12%, *or* RSI-mod down more than 25-30%, *or* both tests down by the consecutive red cut (PP/BM 7%, RSI-mod 15%).
- **Strategy-only pattern** (RSI-mod amber, PP/BM green): report as "timing slowed, output held". For the lift, keep intensity and trim volume or jumps. For the coach note, use "monitor", not "modify".

---

## Where Baylor's numbers and the literature agree or conflict

| Point | Literature | Baylor | Agree / conflict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Noise ranking | Conc. impulse < PP < JH < CT/FT:CT/RSI-mod < ecc. RFD [Zotero: BAV77QQL, pp. 5-8; QJ2IG6CA, pp. 4-5] | 2.9 < 3.8 < 5.7 < 8.8 RSI-mod; ecc. decel RFD 18.4 | **Agree** |
| RSI-mod reliability | CV 10-12%; "poor" [Zotero: 6KR3ZVIW, abstract] | TE 8.8%, SWC/TE 0.48 | **Agree** |
| Which metric is "best" | Strategy metrics (RSI-mod, FT:CT, durations) most *sensitive* | PP/BM best *signal-to-noise* | **Apparent conflict. Not a real one.** Literature reports signal size, mostly 0-24 h after lab protocols or other codes. Baylor reports week-to-week noise, and its "responsiveness" is the Mon->Thu weekly rhythm (+0.90% PP), not a post-game response. Neither has measured post-game signal / noise per metric at 48 h in this population. |
| Peaking synthesis vs metric switch | Flint synthesis bottom line 3: read strategy metrics (mRSI, FT:CT), not jump height alone | Switched readiness flag to PP/BM (2026-07-22) | **Tension** that the two-metric design resolves: PP/BM to flag, RSI-mod for strategy. |
| Baseline | Pre-season or individual SD bands [Zotero: IGW9WRQB; QQD4DSC4] | Earliest-ever test | **Conflict.** Re-anchor each camp; weekday-specific |
| Weekday pooling | Not addressed | Same-weekday pairing required | Draft tree compares Mon and Wed to one baseline: **fix** |
| IMTP RFD noise | Post-AFL RFD CV 16.4% [Zotero: QVA76AQK, via Flint synthesis] | IMTP RFD TE 24-37% | **Agree**: RFD is not usable for weekly decisions |

**Most valuable next analysis (interpretation).** From existing 2023-25 data:
1. For each metric, compute the mean Monday (post-game) change from a same-weekday, non-game-week baseline, divided by that metric's TE.
2. Compute the same for Wednesday.
3. Split by position band and snaps.

That post-game signal-to-noise ratio is the missing number that decides between PP/BM and RSI-mod as primary. Baylor's 2023-25 schedule had CMJ on Thursday and IMTP on Monday, so Monday post-game CMJ data may be sparse. The new Monday CMJ is what will fill this gap.

---

## Gaps

- No 48 h post-game CMJ data in college or NFL football. No NFL time course at all.
- No trial in any football code showing CMJ-guided modification changes injury or performance.
- Most sensitivity evidence uses small samples: n = 5 (Lewis), n = 8-11 (Gathercole), n = 29 (Talpey).
- Most sensitivity evidence also comes from non-match protocols or other codes (AFL, rugby, basketball, futsal).
- Baylor has no typical error for contraction time, FT:CT or countermovement depth. Add them to `src.research.measurement`.
- Unknown whether Baylor TE was computed from best or mean trials.
- Zotero items read only as abstracts: Aychman 2026, Palanisamy 2026, Merrigan 2024, Merrigan 2020. Merrigan 2024 is `indexed-full-text` only.
- Not in Zotero, so worth adding: Anicic 2023, Talpey 2025/2026, Kruczek 2026 (both), Hagstrom 2018, Davis 2021, Rowell 2018, Cormack 2008 reliability.

---

# CMJ fatigue metrics: evidence review for the Monday/Wednesday decision tree

**Question.** Which VALD ForceDecks CMJ metrics (2 jumps, hands on hips, lift warm-up, Monday about 48 h post-game and Wednesday about 72 h pre-kickoff) best detect neuromuscular fatigue in NCAA Division I American football players? The answer should be good enough to flag players for practice modification (reported to position coaches) and to modify the Monday and Wednesday lifts.

**Prepared:** 2026-11-05. Zotero first (via `zotero-bridge`), external peer-reviewed sources labelled `[External]`. No athlete-identifiable data.

**How to read the tags.**
- `[Zotero: KEY, p. N]`: page-located in Eric's library. Page numbers are **bridge PDF page indices**, not printed page numbers. For dissertations they differ: Lewis PDF p. 96 = printed p. 78; Peterson PDF p. 89 = printed p. 78.
- `[Zotero: KEY, abstract]`: in the library, but only the abstract or metadata was read.
- `[External]`: not in Zotero; link given.
- `[Baylor]`: the department's own analysis files (2023-25 ForceDecks data, 185 athletes, 5,930 retest pairs per metric).
- Every claim is also labelled **(finding)** for a direct study result, **(synthesis)** for a cross-paper conclusion, or **(interpretation)** for practitioner judgement.

---

## Practical answer

1. **Keep one output metric and one strategy metric. Drop the rest as flags.**
   - Primary output metric: **Peak Power / BM**.
   - Strategy metric: **RSI-modified**, with a much wider, noise-calibrated threshold.
   - Explain-only metrics (shown, never flagged): **jump height (Imp-Mom)**, **contraction time / time to take-off**, **eccentric duration**, **countermovement depth** (also a protocol QC check).
   - Drop as flag inputs: eccentric deceleration RFD, concentric impulse, mean force, and contraction time on its own.
2. **The draft thresholds are not defensible as written.** One % cut (-6.5 / -10) is applied to three metrics whose noise differs by more than 2x.
   - On RSI-mod, Baylor's own data show the -10% RED rule fires on about **18% of noise-only comparisons**.
   - The -6.5% AMBER boundary sits at about half an SD of week-to-week RSI-mod noise, so it would turn roughly **30%** of healthy tests amber.
   - On Peak Power / BM the same numbers land near Baylor's already-calibrated yellow and orange cuts.
   - CT +5-8% sits inside one CV of CT noise.
   - Replace the cuts with the department's false-positive-calibrated ladder (PP/BM: 7 / 11 / 12%; RSI-mod: 15 / 25 / 30%), plus a **two-test rule** (Monday and Wednesday both down), against **weekday-specific baselines**.
3. **Use the mean of the 2 jumps, not the best.** Add a third jump when the two disagree.
4. **The tool is decision support, not a proven intervention.** No trial in any football code shows that CMJ-guided load modification reduces injury or improves game performance. The evidence for detection is moderate. The evidence that acting on a flag helps is close to none.

---

## Q1. Sensitivity versus reliability, metric by metric

### The "outcome vs strategy" point (synthesis)

Fatigue can leave the jump **outcome** (height, power) intact while changing **how** the jump is made (longer contraction and eccentric time, lower FT:CT or RSI-mod).

- Gathercole 2015 (11 male college team-sport athletes, running fatigue protocol, not a match) **(finding)**:
  - At 72 h, flight time changed only -0.7% while FT:CT fell -7.7% and total duration rose 7.6% [Zotero: NAFZ3EN2, p. 7].
  - In the results table, jump height at 72 h was a trivial *increase* (ES +0.18), while FT:CT was a small decrease (ES -0.44) [Zotero: NAFZ3EN2, p. 8].
  - The authors advise adding "variables that reflect the NM strategy used" [Zotero: NAFZ3EN2, p. 2].
- In DI football, CMJ jump height rose significantly by 72 h post-game, while match load slowed the recovery of RSI-mod and time to take-off [External: Talpey et al. 2026] **(finding)**.
- Bishop et al. 2023 conclude that jump height and peak power "may be less sensitive" to fatigue than time-based metrics (time to peak power, FT:CT, which is "essentially the same as RSI_Mod", and time to take-off) [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, pp. 3-4] **(synthesis, narrative review)**.
  - Bishop cites Claudino 2017 as finding ES -0.04 for maximal JH and PP after fatiguing protocols. That is Bishop's reading; the Claudino pages read here do not show it directly.

### Ranking table

How the columns were built:
- **Sensitivity**: literature effect sizes after match or fatigue.
- **Lit. reliability**: inter-session CV / ICC, no arm swing, from Heishman 2020 [Zotero: BAV77QQL, Tables 4, 6, 8, pp. 5-8], DI basketball, ForceDecks.
- **Baylor TE**: week-to-week typical error and SWC/TE [Baylor: `cmj_measurement_properties.md`].

| Rank for this tool | Metric | Sensitivity to fatigue (literature) | Lit. reliability (CV%, ICC) | Baylor TE % (SWC/TE) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Peak Power / BM** | Moderate. PP fell after contact-code matches (SMD -0.80 at 24 h) [External: Hagstrom & Shorter 2018]. Youth AF PP down to 68 h [External: Davis 2021]. Weaker after lab protocols per Bishop [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 3]. | Abs PP 3.7%, ICC 0.96 | **3.8 (0.78)**, best ratio of 10 | **Primary output flag** |
| 2 | **RSI-mod** (Imp-Mom) | High. Large drops 0-24 h after a football lift session (ES -1.24 / -1.05; n = 5) [Zotero: 8XYJQFMV, PDF p. 97]. Match load slowed its recovery in DI football [External: Talpey 2026]. Linked to biomarker strain mid-season [Zotero: GZBHYCNM, abstract]. | 10.4%, ICC 0.85; Mercer 11.7% (mean of 3) [Zotero: QJ2IG6CA, p. 5]; "poor test-retest" [Zotero: 6KR3ZVIW, abstract] | **8.8 (0.48)** | **Strategy flag**, wide threshold only |
| 3 | FT:CT | High; the classic AFL marker: reduced on 60% of in-season occasions, up to -17% [Zotero: IGW9WRQB, p. 1]. Same construct as RSI-mod [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 4]. | 9.3%, ICC 0.78 | not measured | Redundant with RSI-mod; pick one |
| 4 | Jump height (Imp-Mom) | Low-moderate. Can hold or rise while strategy degrades (above). Rugby union meta: small non-significant drops at 24/48 h [Zotero: CNJETVCQ, p. 1]. | 5.4%, ICC 0.94 | 5.7 (0.63) | Context only (it is the numerator of RSI-mod) |
| 5 | Contraction time / time to take-off | Moderate-high. Large duration increases after fatigue [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 4]. Match-load effect in DI football [External: Talpey 2026]. | 8.5%, **ICC 0.61**. TTT "not reliable" in DI football [External: Talpey 2025] | not measured | Explainer, not a flag |
| 6 | Eccentric duration | High acutely (ES 1.91-1.93) [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 4; 8XYJQFMV, PDF p. 97] | 11.7%, **ICC 0.52** | 6.6 (0.42) | Explainer |
| 7 | Countermovement depth | A strategy dimension (its own principal component in DI football) [Zotero: 7KY6KMGR, p. 1]. Depth changes the output metrics [Zotero: K9IX3SMP, abstract]. | (not in Heishman) | not measured | **QC check**: a depth change of more than a few cm invalidates the comparison |
| 8 | Concentric impulse | Low. Baylor mean Mon->Thu change +0.06%, "inert" | 2.7%, ICC 0.98 | 2.9 (0.99) | Drop. Quiet because nothing moves it; absolute value tracks body mass |
| 9 | Ecc. deceleration RFD / impulse | Fell after basketball practice [Zotero: A2Y3BKFY, abstract] | **26.3%**. Mercer RFD 18.5%, decel *impulse* 7.7% [Zotero: QJ2IG6CA, p. 4]. Ecc RFD and impulse unreliable intrasession [Zotero: MUJBA4LK, abstract]. RFD biased across systems [Zotero: 6KR3ZVIW, abstract] | 18.4 (0.42) | Drop RFD. Decel impulse is the only eccentric candidate worth a local test |
| 10 | Mean force (ecc. mean force) | Very low; approximately body weight | 0.8%, ICC 0.995 | not measured | Drop. Reliable because it barely measures anything |

**Rank order agrees (synthesis).** Baylor's noise ranking and the literature's agree closely:
- Concentric impulse is quietest.
- PP next.
- Then JH.
- Then the timing and ratio metrics.
- Eccentric RFD is the worst.

Heishman, Mercer, Merrigan 2024 and Baylor all put RSI-mod among the noisier metrics.

---

## Q2. Are the -6.5% / -10% thresholds defensible?

**Short answer: no, not as one cut across three metrics.** The cuts happen to be roughly right for Peak Power / BM and wrong for RSI-mod. For contraction time they are uncalibrated.

### What a cut costs in false flags (synthesis, computed from Baylor's numbers)

Method:
- Approximate one-sided rate at which a noise-only change exceeds the cut, assuming normal change scores.
- RSI-mod and PP/BM change-score SDs from [Baylor: `readiness_metric_switch.md`]: 13.09% and 5.40%.
- JH change-score SD estimated as TE x sqrt(2) = 8.1%.
- These are approximations. Baylor's empirical figure is the one to trust where it exists.

| Draft cut | RSI-mod | Jump height | PP/BM (for comparison) |
|---|---|---|---|
| AMBER at -6.5% to -7% | about 30% of healthy tests | about 20% | about 10% (near Baylor's calibrated *yellow*, >7%) |
| RED at -10% | about 22% normal approximation; **18.2% empirical** [Baylor] | about 11% | about 3% (between Baylor yellow and orange) |
| CT AMBER +5-8% | Inside one inter-session CV (8.5%, ICC 0.61) [Zotero: BAV77QQL, p. 6] | | |

- **(finding, Baylor)** The old ">10% -> red" RSI-mod rule meant "roughly one red in five was measurement noise". Recalibrating to equal false-positive rates gives RSI-mod 15 / 25 / 30% and PP/BM 7 / 11 / 12% (single test), with consecutive-test cuts of 5 / 10 / 15% and 2.5 / 5 / 7% [Baylor: `readiness_metric_switch.md`].
- **(interpretation)** The Wednesday cuts (-6 / -11%) have no separate evidence base. Noise does not change by weekday. Only the action on a Wednesday flag differs.

### Individual SWC / CV / z-scores vs fixed % cuts

- **(synthesis)** The literature recommends athlete-specific baselines with distribution-based thresholds (SD bands, minimal detectable change), chosen with explicit Type I / Type II trade-offs [Zotero: QQD4DSC4, pp. 1-2].
  - Claudino 2016 autoregulated training with the individual "minimal individual difference" in CMJ height [Zotero: T6EYDYN3, p. 1].
- **(finding, Baylor)** No CMJ metric resolves the 0.2 x between-athlete-SD SWC at individual week-to-week resolution (all SWC/TE < 1) [Baylor: `cmj_measurement_properties.md`].
- **(interpretation)** For *fatigue* detection the right yardstick is noise (TE), not SWC. A flag should mean "this drop is bigger than normal week-to-week variation".
  - Reported post-game and post-fatigue changes are about the same size as one TE. Examples: FT:CT -7.7% [Zotero: NAFZ3EN2, p. 7]; RSI-mod / CMRJ effects d of about 0.5 at 24 h [External: Talpey 2026].
  - So a **single** test can only catch large drops. Repeated or consecutive tests are the usable unit, as the measurement doc concludes.
- **(interpretation, Baylor)** Per-athlete SDs need many tests. At 8-12 observations per athlete, Baylor found the standard individual-response test rejects the null 90.7% of the time under no effect.
  - Practical consequence: use **pooled (position-band) TE** to set thresholds, then express each player's change against his own baseline. Do not trust individual SDs until a player has 10+ same-weekday tests.
- **% cut vs z-score.** A % cut is fine *if* it is derived from that metric's TE. Baylor's ladder is exactly that and is easier for coaches to read than a z-score.

### Rolling vs fixed baselines

- **(finding)** Cormack 2008 compared weekly values with a pre-season baseline. FT:CT reductions against it tracked periods of fatigue across a 22-match AFL season [Zotero: IGW9WRQB, pp. 1, 13].
- **(finding, Baylor)** The shipped readiness baseline is "each athlete's earliest test" [Baylor: `readiness_metric_switch.md`].
  - **(interpretation)** For returning players this anchor can be years old. Training adaptation then hides fatigue, or a strength gain looks like readiness.
- **(finding, Baylor)** Same-weekday pairing is deliberate: Monday and Thursday differ in weekly rhythm, and pooling them overstates TE [Baylor: `cmj_measurement_properties.md`].
- **Recommendation (interpretation).** A **weekday-specific** baseline:
  - Monday is compared with Mondays, Wednesday with Wednesdays.
  - Each is the mean of that player's last 4-6 non-flagged same-weekday tests (rolling).
  - It is re-anchored each fall camp, with a season-start reference kept alongside so slow drift (chronic decline) stays visible.
  - A pure rolling baseline can absorb accumulating fatigue. The camp anchor is the guard against that.

### How many reps: best vs mean of 2

- **(finding)** Meta-analysis of 151 studies: average CMJ height was more sensitive than highest CMJ height for detecting fatigue and supercompensation. All comparisons favoured the average [Zotero: SCL9W3QP, pp. 1, 4].
- **(finding)** In professional basketball, mean of 3 had lower inter-day CV than best-JH trial for 79 of 84 variables. Mean of 3 gave seasonal signal above noise for 77 of 84 variables, against 65 for best-JH and 58 for best-FT:CT [Zotero: QJ2IG6CA, pp. 1, 3].
- **(finding)** Two maximal CMJs on force plates gave acceptable intrasession reliability for most metrics in DI athletes, except RFD, eccentric impulse and stiffness [Zotero: MUJBA4LK, abstract].
- **(finding)** Across a 6-jump clustered protocol (314 athletes), the best output trial most often came on rep 4, not rep 1 or 2 [External: Kruczek et al. 2026, *J Sports Sci*].
  - **(interpretation)** "Best of 2" is a biased sample of the true best. The mean of 2 is the more honest estimate.
- **Recommendation.** Mean of 2. Add a 3rd jump when the two differ in jump height by more than about 5%, or when depth differs visibly.
- **Open question for Baylor:** were the TE figures computed on best or mean trials? The thresholds should be built on the same summary the tool uses.

---

## Q3. American football evidence: post-game time course and in-season monitoring

| Study | Population / design | What it shows | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Talpey et al. 2026, *JSCR* 40(6):682-688 | 29 DI players, 2 games; CMJ and rebound CMJ at -24 h, +24 h, +72 h; dual force plates; GPS PlayerLoad | **(finding)** Rebound-CMJ power, RSI-mod and JH fell at 24 h (d 0.46-0.67), with power recovered by 72 h. CMJ JH *increased* by 72 h. Match load mediated recovery of CMJ RSI-mod (p = 0.004) and time to take-off (p = 0.016). | [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000005386) |
| Talpey et al. 2025, *JSCR* 39(2):200-209 | 46 DI players, 3 days | **(finding)** Most CMJ variables reliable *except time to take-off*. Rebound-phase CVs >10%. | [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000004969) |
| Kraemer et al. 2009; Sterczala et al. 2014 | DI, starters vs DNP; game 9 | **(finding)** CK and myoglobin raised at 18-20 h and back near pre-game by 42-44 h (Monday), with stable hormones. No jump data. | [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0b013e31819306f2), [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/jsc.0000000000000467) |
| Davis et al. 2021, *JSCR* | 13 *youth* AF players, one game, 7 days | **(finding)** CMJ PP, JH and take-off velocity down up to 68 h; flight time up to 44 h. | [External](https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000004011) |
| Lewis (dissertation, 2021) | 5 college AF players, **post-training session, not a game** | **(finding)** FT:CT and RSI-mod large drops at 0 h (ES -1.20 / -1.24) and still at 24 h (-1.08 / -1.05). JH only small at 24 h (-0.27). | [Zotero: 8XYJQFMV, PDF pp. 96-98] |
| Aychman et al. 2026, *Front Physiol* | 39 DI players, 15-week season | **(finding)** Mid-season CMJ declines alongside biomarker changes. Non-starters showed more strain despite lower load. Exploratory, one program. | [Zotero: GZBHYCNM, abstract] |
| Merrigan et al. 2022, *JSCR* | 82 DI players, 2 no-arm-swing CMJs | **(finding)** Linemen have longer propulsive durations and lower RSI-mod than skill players. Four components: explosive transfer (RSI-mod), eccentric loading, countermovement strategy, height/power. | [Zotero: 7KY6KMGR, p. 1] |
| Peterson (dissertation, 2024) | DI football, 4 seasons | **(finding, exploratory)** More than 10% drop in an SSC factor at baseline linked to traumatic lower-extremity injury, OR 6.49 (90% CI 1.22-34.38, p = 0.065). The simpler model fit as well (LRT p = 0.76). No in-season NFOR x week effect. Hypothesis-generating only. | [Zotero: UWCY55NG, PDF pp. 4, 89, 93] |
| Hagstrom & Shorter 2018 | Meta-analysis, contact football codes | **(finding)** CMJ PP down immediately (SMD -0.59) and at 24 h (-0.80). CK up to 48 h. | [External](https://doi.org/10.1080/17461391.2018.1480661) |

**Not found** (Zotero or external search):
- No college or NFL CMJ data at exactly **48 h** post-game. That is the Monday slot. Talpey is 24 and 72 h. Kraemer is CK at 42-44 h.
- No **NFL** post-game CMJ time course.
- Nothing on CMJ at the Wednesday (~96 h post-game) slot.

**(synthesis)** The 48 h status has to be interpolated. Output metrics in college players are mostly back by 72 h, and some overshoot. Strategy metrics recover more slowly and depend on game load. Monday is the slot where a strategy-metric flag is most likely to be real.

**(interpretation)** Football position groups differ enough that thresholds and baselines should be position-band aware [Zotero: 7KY6KMGR, p. 1]. Snap count belongs in the context column [External: Talpey 2026; Zotero: GZBHYCNM, abstract].

---

## Q4. Does CMJ-guided load modification change outcomes?

- **Only controlled trial found (finding).** U17 futsal, 9 vs 9, randomised. Training load autoregulated from mean CMJ height and each player's minimal individual difference. The regulated group overreached more, then rose above baseline after the taper (ES 0.30); controls did not change [Zotero: T6EYDYN3, p. 1].
  - The outcome was the CMJ itself, not game performance or injury.
- **Associations with match output (finding).** Some evidence links CMJ status to on-field output:
  - AFL players flagged "fatigued" by FT:CT had a -5.8% vertical-vector contribution to accelerometer load and less high-speed running [Zotero: QQXUXWCX, PDF p. 4].
  - FT:CT showed a small correlation with coach-rated performance (r = 0.24) [Zotero: IGW9WRQB, p. 1].
- **Against (finding).** In A-League soccer, training-load effects on pre-match FT:CT were "mostly unclear or trivial" [External: Rowell et al. 2018].
  - **(finding, Baylor)** Six attempts to detect a practice-load effect on readiness returned nothing [Baylor: `cmj_measurement_properties.md`].
- **Injury.** Only Peterson's exploratory association (above). Bishop notes peak power did not predict future injury in rugby league or AFL [Zotero: 5W6F3SHM, p. 4].
- **Caution (synthesis).** Kruczek et al. 2026 argue that readiness flags get too much decision weight in under-prepared athletes. Repeatedly cutting training for "trivial short-term fluctuations" erodes the capacity the athlete still needs [External: Kruczek, Rebelo, Gabbett, Nowak 2026, *Front Physiol*].
  - **(interpretation)** In football terms: a red on a low-snap player should change *what* he does, not just reduce it.

**(synthesis) Verdict.** The CMJ detects fatigue. There is no evidence that modifying practice or lifts on a CMJ flag improves injury rates or game performance in any football code. Build the tool as decision support, and log every flag with the action taken, so Baylor can later compare flagged-and-modified with flagged-and-not-modified.

---

## Q5. Recommended metric set

| Role | Metric | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary output** | **Peak Power / BM** (mean of 2) | Lowest noise with a usable response in Baylor's data (TE 3.8%, best SWC/TE) [Baylor]. Literature reliability agrees (CV 3.7%, ICC 0.96) [Zotero: BAV77QQL, p. 5]. Sensitive to contact-code matches at 24 h [External: Hagstrom 2018]. Already the department's readiness metric, so the tool and the readiness flag agree. |
| **Strategy 1** | **RSI-mod** (Imp-Mom) | The most fatigue-sensitive metric in football and team-sport data [Zotero: 8XYJQFMV, PDF p. 97; External: Talpey 2026; Zotero: IGW9WRQB, p. 1]. Catches the "height held, timing slowed" pattern. Too noisy for a tight cut (TE 8.8%), so flag only on Baylor's RSI-mod ladder (15 / 25 / 30%) or on two consecutive tests. |
| **Strategy 2 (explain only)** | **Contraction time** (or eccentric duration) | When RSI-mod drops and JH holds, CT says the timing moved. Shown on the report but never flagged alone: ICC 0.61 [Zotero: BAV77QQL, p. 6], TTT unreliable in DI football [External: Talpey 2025]. |
| **QC** | Countermovement depth | A changed depth changes every timing metric [Zotero: K9IX3SMP, abstract; 7KY6KMGR, p. 1]. Re-jump, or mark the test non-comparable. |
| **Drop** | Eccentric deceleration RFD; concentric impulse; mean force; FT:CT as a separate metric; jump height as a separate flag | Unreliable (RFD), inert (impulse), insensitive (mean force), or redundant (FT:CT, JH, which are already inside RSI-mod). |

**Flag logic (interpretation, built on Baylor's calibration):**
- **GREEN**: PP/BM and RSI-mod both within the yellow cut against the same-weekday baseline.
- **AMBER**: PP/BM down more than 7%, *or* RSI-mod down more than 15%, *or* both Monday and Wednesday down by the consecutive cuts (PP/BM 2.5-5%, RSI-mod 5-10%).
- **RED**: PP/BM down more than 11-12%, *or* RSI-mod down more than 25-30%, *or* both tests down by the consecutive red cut (PP/BM 7%, RSI-mod 15%).
- **Strategy-only pattern** (RSI-mod amber, PP/BM green): report as "timing slowed, output held". For the lift, keep intensity and trim volume or jumps. For the coach note, use "monitor", not "modify".

---

## Where Baylor's numbers and the literature agree or conflict

| Point | Literature | Baylor | Agree / conflict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Noise ranking | Conc. impulse < PP < JH < CT/FT:CT/RSI-mod < ecc. RFD [Zotero: BAV77QQL, pp. 5-8; QJ2IG6CA, pp. 4-5] | 2.9 < 3.8 < 5.7 < 8.8 RSI-mod; ecc. decel RFD 18.4 | **Agree** |
| RSI-mod reliability | CV 10-12%; "poor" [Zotero: 6KR3ZVIW, abstract] | TE 8.8%, SWC/TE 0.48 | **Agree** |
| Which metric is "best" | Strategy metrics (RSI-mod, FT:CT, durations) most *sensitive* | PP/BM best *signal-to-noise* | **Apparent conflict. Not a real one.** Literature reports signal size, mostly 0-24 h after lab protocols or other codes. Baylor reports week-to-week noise, and its "responsiveness" is the Mon->Thu weekly rhythm (+0.90% PP), not a post-game response. Neither has measured post-game signal / noise per metric at 48 h in this population. |
| Peaking synthesis vs metric switch | Flint synthesis bottom line 3: read strategy metrics (mRSI, FT:CT), not jump height alone | Switched readiness flag to PP/BM (2026-07-22) | **Tension** that the two-metric design resolves: PP/BM to flag, RSI-mod for strategy. |
| Baseline | Pre-season or individual SD bands [Zotero: IGW9WRQB; QQD4DSC4] | Earliest-ever test | **Conflict.** Re-anchor each camp; weekday-specific |
| Weekday pooling | Not addressed | Same-weekday pairing required | Draft tree compares Mon and Wed to one baseline: **fix** |
| IMTP RFD noise | Post-AFL RFD CV 16.4% [Zotero: QVA76AQK, via Flint synthesis] | IMTP RFD TE 24-37% | **Agree**: RFD is not usable for weekly decisions |

**Most valuable next analysis (interpretation).** From existing 2023-25 data:
1. For each metric, compute the mean Monday (post-game) change from a same-weekday, non-game-week baseline, divided by that metric's TE.
2. Compute the same for Wednesday.
3. Split by position band and snaps.

That post-game signal-to-noise ratio is the missing number that decides between PP/BM and RSI-mod as primary. Baylor's 2023-25 schedule had CMJ on Thursday and IMTP on Monday, so Monday post-game CMJ data may be sparse. The new Monday CMJ is what will fill this gap.

---

## Gaps

- No 48 h post-game CMJ data in college or NFL football. No NFL time course at all.
- No trial in any football code showing CMJ-guided modification changes injury or performance.
- Most sensitivity evidence uses small samples: n = 5 (Lewis), n = 8-11 (Gathercole), n = 29 (Talpey).
- Most sensitivity evidence also comes from non-match protocols or other codes (AFL, rugby, basketball, futsal).
- Baylor has no typical error for contraction time, FT:CT or countermovement depth. Add them to `src.research.measurement`.
- Unknown whether Baylor TE was computed from best or mean trials.
- Zotero items read only as abstracts: Aychman 2026, Palanisamy 2026, Merrigan 2024, Merrigan 2020. Merrigan 2024 is `indexed-full-text` only.
- Not in Zotero, so worth adding: Anicic 2023, Talpey 2025/2026, Kruczek 2026 (both), Hagstrom 2018, Davis 2021, Rowell 2018, Cormack 2008 reliability.

---

input.message:
The draft thresholds are not defensible, and the best set is Peak Power / BM as the main flag plus RSI-mod for jump timing. The full findings are at /Users/kristinarash/DEV/Football/Gemini_Projects/docs/research/cmj_fatigue_metrics_evidence.md. I did not commit it (you said not to; the repo's AGENTS.md routine says commit and push, so that call is yours).

**Ranked metrics for this tool** (Baylor's week-to-week noise in brackets):
1. Peak Power / BM (3.8%, best of the 10 metrics)
2. RSI-mod (8.8%; picks up fatigue best but is noisy)
3. FT:CT (same measure as RSI-mod)
4. Jump height (5.7%; can hold or even rise while timing slows)
5. Contraction time / time to take-off (unreliable)
6. Eccentric duration (unreliable)
7. Countermovement depth (use as a quality check)
8. Concentric impulse (quiet because nothing moves it)
9. Eccentric deceleration RFD (18-26% noise)
10. Mean force (reliable only because it is roughly body weight)

Baylor's noise ranking matches the published data almost exactly. The apparent conflict, where papers favour timing metrics and Baylor favours Peak Power / BM, is not real. Papers report how big the fatigue drop is. Baylor measured week-to-week noise. Nobody has measured the post-game drop against the noise at 48 h in this population.

**Threshold verdict.** One cut across three metrics with different noise is the core problem.
- On RSI-mod, the -10% RED rule fires on 18.2% of noise-only comparisons (Baylor's own figure).
- The -6.5% AMBER line would turn about 30% of healthy tests amber (my estimate from Baylor's noise figures).
- On Peak Power / BM the same cuts land near Baylor's calibrated yellow and orange.
- CT +5-8% sits inside one CV of CT noise.
- The fix:
  - Use the department's calibrated ladder: Peak Power / BM 7 / 11 / 12%, RSI-mod 15 / 25 / 30%, plus a Monday-and-Wednesday-both-down rule.
  - Compare Mondays only with Mondays and Wednesdays only with Wednesdays. Reset the baseline each fall camp, not from the earliest-ever test.
  - Use the mean of the 2 jumps, not the best; add a third jump when they disagree.
- Baylor's consecutive cuts were set on same-weekday pairs, so they are borrowed for the Mon+Wed rule, not calibrated for it.

**Recommended set.**
- **Main flag:** Peak Power / BM.
- **Timing flag:** RSI-mod, wide threshold only.
- **Shown but never flagged:** contraction time and countermovement depth (depth doubles as a protocol check).
- **Drop as flag inputs:** eccentric deceleration RFD, concentric impulse, mean force, FT:CT, and jump height as a separate flag.

**Most important citations:**
- Heishman 2020 [Zotero BAV77QQL]: noise and reliability for each metric, no arm swing, ForceDecks.
- Gathercole 2015 [Zotero NAFZ3EN2]: at 72 h jump height held while FT:CT fell 7.7%.
- Talpey 2026 [External, JSCR 40(6)]: Division I football, 29 players; game load slowed RSI-mod and time-to-take-off recovery; jump height rose by 72 h.
- Claudino 2017 [Zotero SCL9W3QP] and Mercer 2023 [Zotero QJ2IG6CA]: the mean of trials beats the best trial.
- Baylor's `readiness_metric_switch.md` and `cmj_measurement_properties.md`.

**Not found:**
- No college or NFL CMJ data at 48 h post-game (Monday); no NFL time course.
- No trial in any football code showing CMJ-guided load changes improve injury or performance. The only controlled trial is U17 futsal with 9 per group, and its outcome was the jump itself.

Peterson 2024's injury link (OR 6.49, p = 0.065) is exploratory only. Four Zotero items were read as abstracts only.

The number that would settle Peak Power / BM versus RSI-mod as the main flag is each metric's Monday post-game change divided by its noise, from Baylor's own data.
